entities.name: Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ala-ud-Din Hasan Bahman Shah, born Zafar Khan, ascended the throne on August 3, 1347, founding the Bahmani Sultanate, a powerful independent Muslim kingdom in the Deccan region of South India that profoundly shaped the subcontinent's political and cultural landscape for nearly two centuries. His reign, lasting until his death on February 19, 1358, marked a definitive break from the increasingly centralized and often oppressive rule of the Delhi Sultanate under Muhammad bin Tughluq, establishing a new regional power center with its own distinct Indo-Persian cultural synthesis.

Having initially served as a governor under the Tughluqs, Hasan Bahman Shah emerged as a leader of the Amiran-i-Sada, a group of disgruntled centurions and local nobles who rebelled against Delhi's authority in the Deccan. Following a series of successful military campaigns, culminating in the capture of Daulatabad, he was crowned Sultan, taking the regal name Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah. He strategically moved his capital from Daulatabad to Gulbarga (Ahsanabad), a more central and defensible location, and rapidly consolidated his nascent kingdom. His early administrative efforts focused on establishing a robust governance structure, dividing the realm into four provinces (tarfs) each under a governor (tarafdar), and initiating the systematic collection of revenue, laying the groundwork for a stable and expansive state.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah's founding of the Bahmani Sultanate fundamentally reshaped the political landscape of the Deccan, establishing an independent Muslim power that endured for nearly two centuries and left a lasting cultural and architectural legacy. His actions led to the prolonged rivalry with the Vijayanagara Empire, defining regional geopolitics for generations.
